newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia holds out olive branch to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Colombia holds out olive branch to rebels.

text.p: The government held out an olive branch to Colombia's leftist rebels on Monday, saying it hoped their release of 70 captive servicemen marked a first step toward settling Latin America's oldest guerrilla war.

But President Ernesto Samper, who said neither side was winning the war, warned against excessive optimism about the possibility of jump-starting peace talks in a country that has been bleeding itself to death for more than three decades.

"I can't propose magic solutions," Samper said in one of several radio interviews. "We've been at war for 35 years and nobody can legtimately say that tomorrow we're going to enter into a whole new era and the country will live in peace."

But he stressed that he sensed "a new will for peace" on the part of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels and he said his government was studying a series of conditions for peace talks set on Sunday by Manuel "Sure Shot" Marulanda, the FARC's veteran commander, in a communique.

Those conditions include the permanent demilitarization of four municipalities in southern Colombia and an end to the Living Together civilian self-defence organisations, which the rebels equate with right-wing paramilitary groups.

In interviews with all three of Colombia's leading news radio stations, Samper seemed to go out of his way to depict Sunday's handover of 70 servicemen -- 60 of whom had been held prisoner by the FARC since Aug. 30, 1996 -- as a victory for the government rather than the result of a humiliating defeat.

The FARC, Colombia's oldest and largest guerrilla force, scored one of its most important political victories by forcing the army to pull out of a 5,000-square-mile (13,000-sq.-km) jungle zone for 32 days to make way for the release.
Samper said the time had come to think in terms of the national interest and not simply of momentary victories or defeats in a conflict that has been stalemated for years.

"We have to be realistic and understand that while it's true we're not losing the war, we're also not winning it," he said. "We've been in a status quo situation for many years now ... in which innocent people are getting the worst end of things. The government has the capacity and at this time the will to sit down and look for new formulas for peace."

Military leaders are sure to bridle at the idea of making any concessions for peace talks with the FARC, which was founded as a pro-Soviet group in 1964. The army insists the FARC is devoid of ideology, calling it a "narco-guerrilla" force of bandits in olive drab that earns millions of dollars annually through kidnapping, extortion and drug trafficking.

But Samper, who noted that he was Colombia's commander in chief, said he was determined to do everything possible to get a peace process under way, even though it was unlikely to end before he stepped down in August 1998.
"Of course, it won't finish under my government," he said. "These are processes that take years."

In an interview with Bogota's El Tiempo newspaper, army commander Gen. Manuel Bonett gave a double-barrelled response when asked if he thought the FARC's handover of his troops opened the door to a possible peace process.
"We have to search for peace," he said. "But to find it, we must first defeat the generators of violence."
